WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Gen. Ray Odierno, the top U.S. military commander in Iraq, said Sunday he believes U.S. troops will be out of the country by the end of 2011. Gen. Ray Odierno says the U.S. is working with Iraq to maintain security improvements as it looks to withdraw. On CNN's "State of the Union," chief national correspondent John King asked Odierno to rate his confidence, on a scale of 1 to 10, that U.S. troops would be out by the end of the timeline agreed by the U.S. and Iraqi governments. "As you ask me today, I believe it's a 10 -- that we will be gone by 2011," Odierno responded. One of the key architects of the troop "surge" strategy in Iraq, Odierno said conditions in the war-torn country have "improved significantly" in the past year or so. "Obviously, we still have some very serious incidents ... but, again, it's much safer," he said. Nine U.S. troops were killed in March, the lowest monthly toll since the beginning of the Iraq War in 2003, he said.  Watch Odierno share his assessment with CNN's John King » . "So, there's been a clear improvement of security here," Odierno said. "The issue is: Can we maintain that? Can the Iraqis maintain it? And that's what we're working through now. We want them to be able to maintain this stability as we pull out." But less than two weeks into April, the U.S. toll for the month is already at nine. Asked whether the attacks were a sign of increased coordinated violence, Odierno responded that "there are some cells out there who are still capable of conducting suicide attacks," though he described the cells as "very small."  Watch as general discusses joining Facebook » . The U.S. military has made it more difficult for foreign fighters to get into Iraq through Syria, but there is still support for the Iraqi insurgency coming from Iran, he said. Mowaffak al-Rubaie, Iraqi national security adviser, said the Iraqi government is making improvements in handling its own security. "We, the government of Iraq and the security forces in Iraq are much more suited now for this fight," al-Rubaie told "State of the Union." "And we believe that now we are leading and we are planning and carrying out most of the combat operations in the country, " he said, "and the United States forces are moving or transitioning to a more support role, more training, more providing more logistical support, rather than engaging in a huge military or kinetic combat operations." Al-Rubaie was mum when asked how President Obama has differed from former President George W. Bush.  Watch al-Rubaie discuss Iraq's future » . "I don't want to elaborate on differences," al-Rubaie said. "But I believe that President Obama understands the situation in Iraq and I believe he wants to stick by ... the withdrawal agreement." Odierno described Obama as "very attentive." "He listens. He's incredibly intelligent. He talks through the issues," Odierno said. "He makes a decision and then we execute those decisions, and that's all you can expect out of your commander-in-chief. And I've been very pleased with the interaction that I've been able to have with him."

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The leading American military official stationed in Iraq, Gen. Ray Odierno, expressed confidence on Sunday that American forces would completely withdraw from the country before 2012 arrives. According to Odierno, the U.S. is collaborating with Iraqi forces to preserve security gains during the withdrawal process.

During an interview on CNN's "State of the Union," senior national correspondent John King pressed Odierno to quantify his certainty—using a 1-to-10 scale—that American forces would depart within the timeframe established by both the U.S. and Iraqi governments. Odierno's reply was unequivocal: "As you ask me today, I believe it's a 10 -- that we will be gone by 2011."

Having played a central role in devising the troop surge strategy, Odierno noted that conditions throughout the conflict-ridden nation had shown substantial improvement over roughly the past year. He acknowledged that dangerous incidents still occur, but emphasized the overall security situation has markedly improved. He pointed out that March saw only nine American fatalities—the smallest monthly death toll recorded since the war began in 2003.

"There's been a clear improvement of security here," the general stated. "The question now is whether we can sustain that progress, and whether the Iraqis themselves can maintain it. That's precisely what we're currently focused on—ensuring they can preserve this stability as our forces depart."

However, with April barely two weeks old, American casualties for the month had already reached nine. When questioned about whether this indicated a rise in organized violence, Odierno acknowledged that certain cells retained the capability to carry out suicide bombings, though he characterized these groups as quite limited in size.

The military has succeeded in restricting the flow of foreign fighters entering Iraq via Syria, Odierno noted, though he indicated that Iran continues providing support to insurgent elements within Iraq.

Mowaffak al-Rubaie, serving as Iraq's national security adviser, remarked that the Iraqi government has strengthened its capacity to manage domestic security matters independently. "We, the government of Iraq and the security forces in Iraq are much more suited now for this fight," he explained to "State of the Union." He added that Iraqi forces now take the lead role in planning and executing the majority of combat missions nationwide, while American troops increasingly shift toward supportive functions—offering training and logistical assistance rather than participating directly in large-scale combat operations.

When questioned about distinctions between President Obama's approach and that of former President George W. Bush, al-Rubaie declined to elaborate. "I don't want to elaborate on differences," he said, though he expressed belief that Obama comprehends the Iraqi situation well and intends to honor the withdrawal timeline that had been agreed upon.

For his part, Odierno characterized Obama as highly engaged and perceptive. "He listens. He's incredibly intelligent. He talks through the issues," the general observed. "He makes a decision and then we execute those decisions, and that's all you can expect out of your commander-in-chief." # U.S. Commander Expresses Strong Confidence in Iraq Withdrawal Timeline

General Ray Odierno, the top U.S. military commander in Iraq, has voiced unequivocal confidence in the timeline for a complete American troop withdrawal from the country. When asked to rate his certainty that U.S. forces would be fully out of Iraq by the end of 2011, Odierno gave the maximum possible assessment—a 10 out of 10—signaling his firm belief that the drawdown will proceed as planned and on schedule.

Odierno, who played an instrumental role in designing and implementing the troop "surge" strategy that helped stabilize Iraq in previous years, pointed to substantial improvements in the security situation over the past twelve months. His firsthand experience shaping that strategy lends particular weight to his assessment of how far the country has come and how sustainable that progress appears to be.

Statistical evidence appears to support this optimistic outlook, at least in part. March recorded the lowest monthly death toll for U.S. troops since the war began in 2003, with only nine American service members losing their lives during that month. However, this positive trend showed signs of reversing quickly, as April's death toll had already matched that same figure—nine fatalities—within just the first two weeks of the month, raising questions about the consistency of the security gains.

Despite the overall positive trajectory, Odierno was candid about the challenges that remain. He acknowledged that small, decentralized terrorist cells continue to possess the capability to carry out suicide attacks, representing an ongoing threat even as larger-scale violence has diminished. Additionally, he noted that Iran continues to provide support to elements of the Iraqi insurgency, complicating efforts to achieve lasting stability. This continued Iranian involvement persists even as the flow of foreign fighters through Syria—once a major conduit for insurgent reinforcements—has been significantly curtailed.

Adding an Iraqi perspective to these assessments, national security adviser Mowaffak al-Rubaie affirmed that the Iraqi government and its security forces are steadily advancing in their capacity to manage the nation's security independently. His comments suggest a growing sense of confidence within Iraqi leadership regarding their ability to assume greater responsibility for the country's stability as American forces prepare for eventual withdrawal, reflecting a shared, if cautious, optimism between U.S. and Iraqi officials about the path forward.

# U.S. Commander Expresses High Confidence in 2011 Iraq Withdrawal Timeline

Gen. Ray Odierno, the top U.S. military commander overseeing operations in Iraq, has voiced strong confidence that American combat forces will complete their withdrawal from the country by the end of 2011, as stipulated under the U.S.-Iraq security agreement. In recent remarks, Odierno rated his confidence level in meeting this timeline as a perfect 10 out of 10, signaling an unusually assertive stance on the pace of the drawdown.

The general's optimism stems largely from measurable improvements in the security situation across Iraq. Notably, March marked a record-low month for American troop deaths since the beginning of the conflict, a milestone that Odierno and other military officials point to as clear evidence that the security gains achieved through the surge strategy—implemented years earlier to quell sectarian violence and insurgent activity—have proven durable and effective over time.

This assessment reflects a broader narrative among U.S. military leadership that the additional troop deployments and counterinsurgency tactics adopted during the surge fundamentally altered the trajectory of the conflict, transforming Iraq from a nation gripped by daily violence into one where security incidents have become increasingly rare and localized.

However, Odierno's confident timeline is not without important caveats. Military officials acknowledge that significant challenges remain in ensuring Iraqi security forces are fully prepared to maintain stability without direct American military support. Chief among these concerns are the continued operations of small, scattered insurgent cells that, while diminished in capability compared to the height of the conflict, still pose a persistent threat to civilian populations and Iraqi government institutions.

Additionally, U.S. officials have expressed ongoing concern about external interference in Iraqi affairs, particularly regarding support and influence originating from Iran. This includes concerns about the funding, training, and equipping of armed groups operating within Iraq that could potentially destabilize the fragile security gains achieved in recent years.

As the 2011 deadline approaches, the challenge for American and Iraqi officials alike will be to build upon the current security momentum while simultaneously strengthening the capacity of Iraqi military and police forces to independently manage these residual threats. The success of this transition will likely serve as a critical test of whether the hard-won stability of recent years can be sustained once U.S. forces have fully departed, marking the true measure of the surge strategy's long-term legacy.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — A growing body of research suggests that Generation Z is reshaping American civic and political life in ways that differ markedly from previous generations, according to analysts and pollsters who spoke with CNN this week.

Born roughly between 1997 and 2012, Gen Z has come of age amid economic uncertainty, a global pandemic, climate anxiety, and unprecedented access to digital information. Experts say these formative experiences are now translating into distinct patterns of civic engagement, voting behavior, and political priorities.

"What we're seeing with Gen Z is a generation that is simultaneously more politically engaged and more skeptical of traditional institutions than any generation before it," said one Washington-based pollster who has studied youth voting trends for over a decade. "They're showing up to vote in significant numbers, but they're also demanding accountability in ways that are reshaping how campaigns and elected officials communicate."

Data from recent election cycles show that young voters — many of them part of Gen Z — have turned out at rates that surprised political strategists in both parties. Issues such as climate change, student debt, gun violence, and reproductive rights consistently rank among their top concerns, according to multiple surveys conducted by nonpartisan research organizations.

Social media platforms have also played an outsized role in shaping how this generation consumes political information. Unlike previous generations who relied primarily on television or print media, Gen Z voters often get their news from platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube — a shift that has forced campaigns and news organizations, including CNN, to adapt their outreach strategies.

Still, experts caution against painting the generation with too broad a brush. "Gen Z is not a monolith," said a political science professor based in Washington. "There's significant diversity in political ideology, regional identity, and lived experience within the generation itself."

As the 2024 election cycle demonstrated, and with future elections on the horizon, both major political parties are increasingly investing resources into understanding and courting Gen Z voters — a demographic whose long-term influence on American democracy is only beginning to take shape.

CNN's political unit will continue monitoring these trends as more data becomes available in the coming months.

counterfactuals.output:
**Gen. Odierno: U.S. on track to meet 2011 Iraq withdrawal deadline**

*(CNN) -- The top U.S. commander in Iraq expressed confidence Sunday that American forces will complete their withdrawal from the country by the end of 2011, telling CNN's "State of the Union" that security gains on the ground support the timeline established in the U.S.-Iraq security agreement.*

Gen. Raymond Odierno, commander of U.S. forces in Iraq, said the drawdown is proceeding according to plan despite ongoing concerns about political instability and sporadic violence in the country.

"I feel very confident about where we are," Odierno told host Candy Crowley. "We've seen significant improvements in the capabilities of the Iraqi security forces, and that gives me confidence that we'll be able to continue this drawdown and complete our mission by the end of 2011."

The remarks come as the U.S. military continues to reduce its footprint in Iraq under the Status of Forces Agreement signed by the Bush administration, which mandates a full withdrawal of American troops by December 31, 2011. President Obama has reaffirmed the deadline while emphasizing a more immediate goal of ending combat operations by August 2010.

Odierno acknowledged that challenges remain, particularly surrounding Iraq's fragile political process and the risk of renewed sectarian tension following parliamentary elections. But he said those concerns should not undermine confidence in the broader trajectory of the mission.

"There will be bumps in the road, there always are," Odierno said. "But structurally, militarily, I think we are exactly where we need to be."

He also addressed concerns about Iraqi security forces' readiness to assume full responsibility for the nation's security, saying they have made "tremendous strides" over the past year, though he noted continued U.S. support -- including training and logistics -- would still be necessary in the near term.

Asked whether he was worried the withdrawal timeline could slip, Odierno was direct: "I don't see that happening. We've planned this very deliberately, and I believe we're going to meet our obligations."

The general's comments echo similar statements from other senior military and administration officials who have sought to reassure the public that the transition in Iraq remains on schedule, even as attention increasingly shifts to the ongoing conflict in Afghanistan.

Odierno's tour as the top commander in Iraq has coincided with a period of relative calm following the surge of U.S. troops in 2007, though attacks in Baghdad and other cities in recent months have raised questions about the durability of the security gains.

Despite that, Odierno maintained an optimistic outlook. "I've been here a long time," he said. "I've seen it at its worst, and I see the progress we've made. I have confidence in this timeline."

*CNN's Elise Labott contributed to this report.*

# Iraq Security Improves as U.S., Iraqi Officials Signal Confidence in Withdrawal Timeline

*Baghdad* — Senior American and Iraqi officials offered an upbeat assessment of Iraq's security situation this week, pointing to continued declines in violence as justification for maintaining the planned withdrawal of U.S. forces from the country.

General Ray Odierno, the top U.S. commander in Iraq, said that security gains achieved over the past year have been largely sustained, crediting improved capabilities within Iraqi security forces alongside continued, though reduced, U.S. support. Odierno noted that attacks remain near historic lows and emphasized that Iraqi forces are increasingly taking the lead on operations across the country, from urban centers to rural provinces.

The general acknowledged that challenges remain, particularly around political reconciliation, disputed territories, and the potential for extremist groups to exploit any security vacuum. However, he expressed confidence that Iraqi forces are prepared to shoulder greater responsibility as U.S. troop levels continue to draw down under the agreed timeline.

Echoing that assessment, Iraqi National Security Adviser Mowaffak al-Rubaie struck a similarly confident tone, stating that Iraqi forces have made significant strides in their ability to independently secure the country. Al-Rubaie pointed to the reduced frequency of large-scale bombings and improved coordination between Iraqi army, police, and intelligence services as evidence of the country's growing self-sufficiency.

Al-Rubaie also addressed the political dimension of the withdrawal, framing it as a matter of national sovereignty as much as security. He reiterated that the Iraqi government remains committed to the timetable for U.S. troop reductions, viewing it as a milestone in Iraq's transition toward full control over its own security affairs.

Both officials cautioned that the drawdown would not be entirely without risk, and that sporadic violence — including attacks by insurgent remnants and sectarian actors — could still occur. However, neither suggested that such incidents would be sufficient to alter the broader trajectory of the withdrawal plan.

The comments come as U.S. and Iraqi officials continue coordinating the phased transfer of security responsibilities ahead of further troop reductions. Analysts note that while security gains have been real and measurable, the durability of Iraq's stability will likely depend heavily on political developments, including efforts to resolve outstanding disputes among Iraq's ethnic and sectarian communities.

Neither Odierno nor al-Rubaie indicated any plans to adjust the current withdrawal schedule, suggesting that both the U.S. and Iraqi governments remain aligned in their assessment that conditions on the ground support continued implementation of the agreed timeline.

*(Note: This report is a general reconstruction based on the type of statements Odierno and al-Rubaie have made publicly on this topic. For precise quotes, dates, and figures, please consult a specific news source or transcript from the original briefing.)*

# Odierno: Iraq Security Gains "Fragile but Real" as Troop Drawdown Continues

BAGHDAD — General Ray Odierno, the top U.S. commander in Iraq, offered a cautiously optimistic assessment of the country's security situation this week, characterizing recent gains as significant but warning against complacency as American forces continue their phased withdrawal.

## Casualty Figures Show Marked Decline

According to military statistics released alongside Odierno's remarks, American combat deaths in Iraq have dropped substantially compared to the height of the conflict. The figures reflect a broader downward trend in violence that has allowed the U.S. to accelerate troop reductions ahead of the 2011 deadline for complete withdrawal established under the U.S.-Iraq Status of Forces Agreement.

Odierno noted that attacks against coalition forces, Iraqi security personnel, and civilians have fallen to levels not seen since the early years of the war. He attributed the improvement to a combination of factors: the increased capability of Iraqi security forces, sustained counterterrorism operations against al-Qaeda in Iraq remnants, and political reconciliation efforts among Iraq's fractured sectarian communities.

Still, the general was careful to temper enthusiasm with realism. "These gains are fragile," he told reporters, emphasizing that sporadic bombings and targeted assassinations remain a persistent threat, particularly in contested areas like Mosul and parts of Diyala province.

## Remarks on President Obama's Strategy

Odierno also addressed President Obama's approach to the drawdown, expressing confidence in the administration's timeline while underscoring the military's role in advising on conditions on the ground.

He described his working relationship with the White House as collaborative, noting that troop withdrawal decisions have been made in close consultation with commanders to ensure that security gains are not jeopardized by an overly hasty exit. Odierno affirmed his support for the president's commitment to ending the U.S. combat mission, while stressing that the drawdown must remain "conditions-based" rather than driven strictly by calendar deadlines.

The general's comments come amid ongoing debate in Washington over the pace of withdrawal and the residual American presence that will remain to train Iraqi forces and conduct limited counterterrorism operations beyond the formal end of combat operations.

## Looking Ahead

Military officials say the coming months will be a critical test of Iraqi forces' ability to maintain security independently, particularly as the U.S. footprint continues to shrink. Odierno reiterated that while the transition carries risk, the trajectory of the past year gives him confidence that Iraq is moving toward greater stability—provided political leaders continue to make progress on outstanding disputes over oil revenue sharing, disputed territories, and national elections.

---

*This report reflects statements and figures attributed to Gen. Odierno during briefings on the security situation in Iraq. Casualty statistics and operational details are subject to periodic revision by the Department of Defense.*

## "State of the Union" Recap: General Odierno Discusses Iraq Withdrawal, Obama's Leadership

*The following is a recreated-style recap in the format of a cable news transcript summary. This is a fictional/illustrative composition.*

---

**ANCHOR:** Thanks for joining us. Today on "State of the Union," retired General Ray Odierno sat down for a wide-ranging conversation covering the drawdown of American forces in Iraq, the security situation on the ground, and his personal assessment of President Obama's leadership style during one of the most consequential military transitions in recent history.

Let's get right to it.

**[BEGIN CLIP]**

**HOST:** General, you oversaw one of the largest logistical drawdowns in modern military history. As you look back, how confident are you that the withdrawal was executed the right way?

**GEN. ODIEROM:** Look, I think we did this methodically. This wasn't a decision made overnight — it was built on conditions on the ground, assessments from commanders, and constant dialogue with Iraqi security forces. Was it a clean, easy process? No. Nothing about Iraq was easy. But I remain confident that the drawdown itself — the movement of personnel, equipment, the transition of responsibility to Iraqi forces — was handled professionally and with discipline.

**HOST:** But there's been criticism that the withdrawal timeline left gaps that contributed to instability down the road.

**GEN. ODIERNO:** I understand that criticism, and it's fair to have that debate. My job, and the job of the military leadership at the time, was to execute the policy decisions that were made and to do everything possible to set the conditions for Iraqi forces to succeed. Whether the pace was right is something historians and policymakers will continue to debate. What I can speak to is the execution — and I stand by how our forces conducted themselves during that period.

**HOST:** Let's talk about the President. You worked closely with President Obama during this period. What was your sense of his approach to these decisions?

**GEN. ODIERNO:** What struck me was his deliberateness. He asked hard questions — not just accepting a plan because it was handed to him, but pushing back, asking "what happens if," "what's the risk here," "what's the alternative." That's what you want from a Commander-in-Chief. He took the responsibility seriously, and he leaned on his commanders for honest assessments, which I appreciated.

**HOST:** Some have described his style as cautious, even hesitant at times. Is that a fair characterization?

**GEN. ODIERNO:** I'd describe it as measured rather than hesitant. There's a difference. He wanted to make sure decisions were sound before committing. In a situation as complex as Iraq, I think that measured approach served the process well, even if it didn't always move as fast as some in the Pentagon might have preferred.

**[END CLIP]**

---

**ANCHOR:** Strong words there from General Odierno — striking a balance between defending the execution of the drawdown while acknowledging the broader debate about timing and strategy. His characterization of President Obama as "measured" rather than "hesitant" is likely to generate discussion among both political commentators and military analysts in the days ahead.

We'll continue to follow reaction to this interview throughout the day. Stay with us for more of "State of the Union" coverage right after this break.
